opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a great question, and the honest answer is that the boundary is a lot blurrier than people sometimes imagine. But let me try to draw it anyway.

The algorithm designer, which is closer to what someone like me does, is asking: suppose you had a perfect, idealized quantum computer, with some number of qubits and the ability to apply gates to them. What problems could you solve dramatically faster than any classical computer? That's where you get things like Shor's algorithm for factoring, Grover's algorithm for search, quantum simulation of chemistry and materials, and so on. In that world, you're working with an abstraction: unit vectors in a Hilbert space, unitary transformations, measurements. You don't care whether the qubits are superconducting loops, trapped ions, neutral atoms, or photons. That abstraction is enormously powerful, just as it was powerful for Turing and von Neumann to think about computation without worrying about vacuum tubes versus transistors.

The hardware engineer is fighting against nature, trying to make that abstraction real. Their enemy is decoherence: the tendency of a quantum system to leak information into its environment, which destroys exactly the interference effects that give you a speedup. So they're worrying about gate fidelities, coherence times, crosstalk, connectivity, and how you scale from dozens of qubits to thousands to millions.

What connects the two worlds is quantum error correction and fault tolerance, one of the great intellectual achievements in this field. The threshold theorem from the 1990s says that if you can get your physical error rate below some threshold, you can use error-correcting codes to simulate a perfect logical qubit with arbitrarily high accuracy, at a cost that grows only polylogarithmically. That theorem is what tells the hardware people their job is "only" finitely hard, and tells the algorithms people they're not just doing fantasy math.

Now, where it gets interesting, and where the division of labor breaks down, is the near-term era we've been living in. When you don't yet have full fault tolerance, you can't just hand off a clean abstraction. You need people who understand both sides: what's the most useful or most clearly classically hard thing you can do with this particular noisy device, with these particular error rates and this particular connectivity? The quantum supremacy experiments, like random circuit sampling, which I was involved in thinking about theoretically, were exactly that kind of co-design. And so was the follow-up, where classical simulation people keep pushing back and trying to spoof the results, and you have this healthy back-and-forth.

I'd add one more thing. The algorithm designer has a responsibility that I think is sometimes neglected, which is to be honest about where the speedups actually are. A lot of hype says quantum computers will revolutionize optimization or machine learning, and when you look carefully, the evidence for big speedups there is much weaker than for, say, simulating quantum systems or breaking certain cryptography. So part of the theorist's job is telling the engineers, and the investors, and the public: here's what this machine you're building is actually going to be good for, and here's what it isn't.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say the division is a lot less clean than people imagine, and it's gotten less clean over time rather than more.

The idealized picture is something like the classical world: the algorithm designer works with an abstract model of computation, like a circuit of gates acting on qubits, proves things about how many operations it takes to solve some problem, and then hands that off to the engineer, whose job is to build a machine that realizes the abstraction. And for a long time, in the nineties and early two-thousands, that's roughly how it worked, because there was no hardware worth speaking of. People like me could sit around proving theorems about Shor's algorithm or Grover's algorithm or quantum query complexity, and the question of whether anyone could build the thing was somebody else's problem, maybe some future generation's problem.

What's changed is that now there are actual devices, with a hundred or a few hundred qubits, and they're noisy, and they have particular connectivity constraints, particular gates that are cheap and particular gates that are expensive. And that means the abstraction leaks. If you want to know what you can actually do with one of these machines, you can't just count gates in the textbook model. You have to know how the error correction works, what the overhead is, which operations are native. So the theorists have had to learn a lot more about the hardware than we used to, and the experimentalists have had to learn a lot more theory, because they need to understand things like what makes a sampling task hard to simulate classically if they want to claim they've done something interesting.

I'd also say the interesting action right now is largely in the middle layer, which is fault tolerance and error correction. That's where the asymptotic questions about which problems have quantum speedups actually meet the questions about what you can fabricate. And the people working there are sort of neither pure algorithm designers nor pure hardware people.

My own role, honestly, has often been less designing algorithms that get run and more figuring out what quantum computers can't do, or what the hardest version of a demonstration is that would still be convincing. So part of the division of labor, at least as I've experienced it, is that the theorists keep the experimentalists honest about what they've actually shown, and the experimentalists keep the theorists honest about what's actually feasible.

astra-6.text:
Well, there’s a division of labor that’s similar to what we have in classical computing. As a quantum algorithm designer, I ask: assuming you have a working quantum computer, what could you do with it? Which problems could you solve faster than we know how to solve them classically? We work with an abstract model—qubits and quantum gates—without necessarily specifying whether those qubits are made from trapped ions, superconducting circuits, or something else.

The hardware engineer’s job is to make those abstractions real: to build qubits that can be controlled precisely, interact in the right ways, and remain coherent long enough to carry out a computation. And, crucially, to get errors low enough that quantum error correction can work.

Of course, the two sides have to talk. An algorithm might be beautiful mathematically but require an absurd number of gates. Hardware constraints can tell us which algorithms are worth pursuing, while algorithms tell the engineers what capabilities would actually be useful. But the abstraction lets us investigate what quantum computers could accomplish before we’ve built a large, reliable one.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a quantum algorithm designer asks, assuming we had a sufficiently reliable quantum computer, what could we do with it? What problems could we solve faster than we know how to solve them classically? You work with an abstract mathematical model of qubits and gates, much as a classical algorithms researcher can work without thinking about how transistors are manufactured.

The hardware engineer asks, how do we actually build a device that realizes those operations? How do we control the qubits, keep them isolated from unwanted interactions, and correct errors well enough to carry out a long computation?

Of course, those questions feed into each other. The hardware determines which operations are expensive and what constraints an algorithm has to respect. And the algorithms tell the engineers what capabilities would actually be useful. So there’s a division of labor, but you need communication across that boundary.
